clusters.cluster: U.S. work stress and burnout among professional women ages 30–55. Priority is qualitative, based on intent fit, breadth, immediacy, and current evidence; it does not claim or infer search volume.
content_gaps: Create a non-diagnostic stress, overload, or possible burnout reflection flow that names exhaustion, cynicism, motivation, concentration, sleep, and work-life spillover; explain it cannot diagnose a condition and give escalation routes.

Pair individual micro-practices with work-design content. Official guidance says excess demands, unclear priorities, low control, bullying, and inadequate resources need organizational responses; do not imply a breathing exercise fixes a harmful workplace.

Provide concise scripts for workload-prioritization, boundary-setting, flexible-schedule, and follow-up conversations. Include alternatives for users who do not feel safe disclosing mental-health details.
Serve the high performer under strain gap: women can be engaged and ambitious while burned out. Do not frame burnout as lack of resilience, commitment, or competence.
Cover caregiving and the mental load without reducing the audience to mothers. Include child care, elder care, disability care, school-calendar coordination, and non-caregiver work overload.
Build a job-insecurity pathway that validates uncertainty, offers grounding and practical preparation prompts, and avoids predicting layoffs, financial outcomes, or career results.
Offer privacy-conscious, low-disclosure support for people worried about stigma, judgment, lost opportunities, or retaliation. Do not say users must disclose health information to an employer.

Use the Apple Watch and iPhone context for brief optional transitions before a difficult meeting, after work, or before sleep. Never claim wearable data can detect burnout. Describe all eight personas as AI wellness guides, not clinicians, friends, or people with lived experience.

evidence_sources.finding: Using Q4 2025 U.S. workforce data from 22,368 employed adults, Gallup reported that 31% of women versus 23% of men felt burned out at work very often or always. Among full-time workers with children, the figures were 33% of women and 25% of men; Gallup also found a persistent burnout gap for women leaders.
evidence_sources.title: Women Show Stronger Employee Engagement Amid Higher Burnout

evidence_sources.finding: The 11th annual report drew on more than 120 companies and 9,000 employees. Six in 10 senior-level women said they frequently felt burned out, compared with half of men at that level and about four in 10 employees overall; it also describes flexibility stigma affecting women who work remotely.
evidence_sources.title: Women in the Workplace 2025

evidence_sources.finding: In an online U.S. survey of 2,017 employed adults conducted March 26 to April 4, 2025, 54% said job insecurity had a significant impact on work stress. The report also links job-loss concerns with sleep and relationship problems and quotes workers citing workload increases and unclear management communication.
evidence_sources.title: Majority of U.S. workers say job insecurity has significant impact on their stress

evidence_sources.finding: Among full-time workers at companies with at least 100 employees, 42% worried their career would be negatively affected if they discussed mental-health concerns at work, only 13% told a manager their mental health was suffering due to work demands in the past year, and one in four had considered quitting because of mental-health concerns.
evidence_sources.publisher: National Alliance on Mental Illness and Ipsos
evidence_sources.title: The 2025 NAMI Workplace Mental Health Poll

evidence_sources.finding: Updated May 12, 2026, CDC lists irritability, uncertainty, lack of motivation, exhaustion, sleep difficulty, and concentration difficulty among stress experiences. It says changing workplace policies and practices is the best way to address burnout and directs people in crisis to call or text 988 or use 988lifeline.org.
evidence_sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
evidence_sources.title: Providing Support for Worker Mental Health

evidence_sources.finding: NIOSH states that chronic occupational stress worsens mental health and recommends addressing environmental determinants and organizational root causes before relying on individual interventions, including greater control, flexibility, supportive supervision, and EAP access.
evidence_sources.publisher: CDC National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
evidence_sources.title: Supporting Mental Health in the Workplace

evidence_sources.finding: OSHA notes that continuing pressure from balancing work with child, elder, medically vulnerable, or disabled-family care can affect mental well-being. It highlights flexibility, compassionate management, caregiving-friendly benefits, and not making workers hide family commitments.
evidence_sources.publisher: U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration
evidence_sources.title: Parents and Other Caregivers

evidence_sources.finding: Mayo Clinic describes job burnout as work-linked stress that can include physical or emotional exhaustion and feelings of powerlessness or emptiness. It explicitly says burnout is not a medical diagnosis and advises speaking with a health or mental-health professional because similar experiences can be linked to other conditions.
evidence_sources.title: Job burnout: How to spot it and take action

safety_notes: State prominently that StressGuru is an iPhone and Apple Watch wellness app. It is not therapy, a healthcare provider, a diagnostic tool, or a substitute for professional medical or mental-health care.

Never diagnose burnout, depression, anxiety, insomnia, or another condition. Use conditional language such as may, can, and might be worth discussing with a qualified professional, especially for persistent sleep changes, hopelessness, substance use, physical symptoms, or impaired daily functioning.

Do not make outcome guarantees or medical claims that an exercise, watch interaction, or AI persona will prevent, treat, cure, detect, or recover burnout. Do not present a self-check, score, or wearable signal as diagnostic.

Describe the eight AI wellness personas only as AI-guided wellness styles or guides. Do not call them clinicians, therapists, credentialed coaches, friends, companions with feelings, or people with lived experience; do not claim they personally understand or experienced the user's situation.

Treat work stress as partly structural. Validate the user without blaming her for workload or asking self-care to compensate for unsafe, discriminatory, abusive, or unsustainable conditions. Do not advise disclosure, confrontation, quitting, or leave as if any result is guaranteed.

Include visible U.S. escalation in high-distress content: for immediate danger or emergency call 911; for suicidal thoughts, crisis, or urgent emotional support call or text 988 or visit 988lifeline.org. Encourage a licensed professional, local emergency service, or trusted support person when appropriate.

Use trauma-informed, stigma-sensitive language. Avoid just relax, fix your mindset, or productivity-shaming. Offer alternatives for users who cannot safely raise concerns with a manager, and avoid legal, HR, benefits, accommodation, or employment-rights conclusions without qualified jurisdiction-specific guidance.

Protect privacy. Do not pressure users to enter identifiable employer, coworker, health, or crisis details, and do not imply that app conversations are privileged, clinical communications or invisible to third parties unless demonstrably true.

clusters.cluster: U.S. intent cluster: high-functioning anxiety, work anxiety, and overthinking for professional women ages 30 to 55. Priority is relative only, not search volume. It ranks exact topical fit, recurrence in current search-result and public-discussion phrasing, practical immediacy, and fit with a brief iPhone or Apple Watch wellness moment. No volume has been asserted or inferred.
content_gaps: Create a plain-English pillar that explains that "high-functioning anxiety" is a commonly used description, not a formal diagnosis. Pair it with a gentle explanation of when persistent worry or symptoms that interfere with life merit a licensed professional's support.

Most high-functioning-anxiety pages list traits. Build a practical professional-woman angle around the cost of appearing fine: overpreparing, extra assignments, post-meeting replay, work-after-hours thought loops, and guilt about boundaries. Treat these as possible experiences, never assumptions about all women.

Make a meeting-to-recovery content series: a 60-second pre-meeting pause, a post-meeting reset, and a next-step note after feedback or a mistake. Keep the promised outcome to a moment of reflection or grounding, not anxiety treatment or improved performance.

Address the work system as well as the individual. CDC guidance favors changes to workload, flexibility, control, and manager support before individual-only interventions. Avoid content that tells the user she alone must self-regulate an unhealthy workplace.

Publish boundary scripts that are calibrated rather than confrontational: asking for priorities, clarifying a deadline, proposing a tradeoff, and deferring a nonurgent request. Include privacy-respecting language for people who do not want to disclose mental-health details at work.

Fill the gap between "overthinking" and "sleep" with a non-medical evening off-ramp: capture tomorrow's action, choose an end-of-day cue, and use an optional short wellness exercise. Do not claim it treats insomnia or stops intrusive thoughts.

Use compassionate mistake-recovery content that distinguishes one repairable action from repeated mental review. Avoid reassurance that a mistake has no consequences, and do not encourage hiding errors or avoiding needed workplace conversations.
Add an explicit help-and-safety module to every cluster hub: ordinary stress can be real, and persistent or distressing symptoms, loss of functioning, or crisis need support beyond an app.

evidence_sources.finding: Describes high-functioning anxiety as a non-DSM term often associated with GAD; people may appear successful while experiencing worry, self-doubt, fear of failure, and overfunctioning such as extra hours or assignments. The page notes women are more than twice as likely as men to experience GAD across their lifetime.
evidence_sources.title: Behind the mask: Managing high-functioning anxiety

evidence_sources.finding: States that high-functioning anxiety is not diagnosable as its own condition. Common outward traits can include high achievement, organization, detail orientation, and proactivity, while inward experiences can include perfectionism, overthinking, reassurance seeking, worst-case thinking, and difficulty saying no.
evidence_sources.title: Signs You Have High-Functioning Anxiety

evidence_sources.finding: Explains that occasional stress and anxiety are normal but anxiety that persists and interferes with daily life warrants professional help. It lists excessive worry, trouble controlling worry, restlessness, concentration difficulty, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep problems, and notes adult concerns can include job performance, finances, and family wellbeing.
evidence_sources.title: Generalized Anxiety Disorder: What You Need to Know

evidence_sources.finding: Updated May 2026, this guidance says chronic stress can worsen health problems and can affect concentration, decisions, sleep, and physical symptoms. It recommends individualized, healthy coping such as breaks, breathing, stretching, journaling, time outdoors, connection, sleep, and physical activity.
evidence_sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
evidence_sources.title: Managing Stress

evidence_sources.finding: Says chronic occupational stress worsens mental health and recommends first addressing organizational root causes, including policies that increase worker flexibility and control, supervisor training, and supportive culture, before relying on individual-level interventions.
evidence_sources.publisher: CDC National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health
evidence_sources.title: Supporting Mental Health in the Workplace

evidence_sources.finding: In a national study of 1,153 U.S. full-time employed adults, half reported moderate to severe burnout, depression, or anxiety. Women reported higher burnout, and workers rated work-life balance and flexibility as the most helpful workplace supports. This is a survey finding, not a clinical prevalence estimate.
evidence_sources.title: 2025 Mental Health at Work Report: Key Workplace Trends

evidence_sources.finding: A January 2025 poll of full-time employees at companies with at least 100 employees found 42% worried that discussing mental-health concerns could harm their career; only 13% said they had told a manager their mental health was suffering due to work demands in the prior year. It also found workers commonly used the terms burnout, stress, and overwhelm more readily than poor mental health.
evidence_sources.publisher: National Alliance on Mental Illness and Ipsos
evidence_sources.title: The 2025 NAMI Workplace Mental Health Poll

evidence_sources.finding: In an online Harris Poll of 3,199 U.S. adults conducted August 4 to 24, 2025, 57% named the rise of AI a major stressor, including 58% of women and 60% of employed adults. The finding supports timely, careful messaging about technology-related stress but does not establish causality or app effectiveness.
evidence_sources.title: Stress in America 2025: A crisis of connection

safety_notes: Use "high-functioning anxiety" as audience language, not a diagnosis. State clearly that StressGuru cannot determine whether someone has anxiety, GAD, another condition, or a medical cause of symptoms.

StressGuru is a wellness app, not therapy, a healthcare provider, crisis care, or a diagnostic tool. Describe its eight AI wellness personas only as AI-guided wellness experiences or styles. Never call them clinicians, therapists, coaches with credentials, people, friends, or beings with lived experience.

Do not promise to treat, cure, prevent, diagnose, reduce clinical anxiety, stop rumination, fix sleep, or improve job performance. Safer language is "may support a brief pause, reflection, grounding, or wind-down practice."

Include an easy-to-find escalation message. NIMH advises professional help when severe or distressing symptoms last two weeks or more or impair usual tasks. For suicidal thoughts, emotional crisis, or immediate danger in the U.S., direct users to call or text 988; in life-threatening emergencies, call 911.

Do not attribute new, severe, or concerning physical symptoms such as breathing difficulty, chest symptoms, faintness, or a racing heart to anxiety. Encourage urgent medical evaluation when appropriate.

Avoid advising users to start, stop, change, or combine medication, alcohol, caffeine, supplements, or treatment. Do not give pregnancy, postpartum, trauma, substance-use, or medical-condition guidance beyond referral to a qualified professional.

Avoid shame, productivity pressure, and forced disclosure. Do not imply that a user can solve a harmful workload through mindset alone, or that she should disclose mental health information, confront an employer, or quit a job.

Use inclusive, conditional language. Professional women may experience caregiving load, relationship demands, financial pressure, or workplace bias, but none should be presumed. Keep privacy and data practices clear, especially before inviting users to record sensitive work or health details.

clusters.cluster: U.S. search-intent cluster for professional women ages 30–55: insomnia, 3 AM waking, and racing thoughts after work. Exact public keyword volume was unavailable in the sources reviewed, so priorities are directional, not volume claims. They reflect exact-cluster fit, recurrence in current Google-style results, specificity, and immediate actionability. The core opportunity is a non-diagnostic path from an after-work wind-down to a low-stimulation middle-of-the-night reset, with clear referral boundaries.
content_gaps: Most 3 AM pages lead with broad cause lists or generic sleep hygiene. Create a three-part path: what to do in the next 10–20 minutes, what to notice over two weeks, and when to talk with a clinician.

Avoid a single-cause cortisol narrative. Give a calm multi-cause explanation that can include light, noise, alcohol, pain, bathroom trips, stress, and possible sleep disorders, with uncertainty stated plainly.
Few search results link a workday-close ritual to the 3 AM moment. Build a paired experience: a five-minute after-work decompression and a separate low-stimulation overnight reset.

Generic journaling advice rarely serves professional work rumination. Offer a brief tomorrow-list, next-tiny-action, and permission-to-revisit-in-daylight exercise, framed as wellness rather than therapy.

Search content often blurs occasional bad sleep and chronic insomnia. Explain the distinction accessibly, including NHLBI's 3 nights per week for more than 3 months definition, and route ongoing impairment to qualified care.

Midlife content often separates menopause from workload and caregiving. Address their overlap without making a hormone or menopause determination; flag night sweats and persistent disruption for clinician discussion.

Work-stress content is commonly daytime-only. Use current APA language about job security, workload increases, unclear communication, and work-life balance without implying the app fixes workplace conditions.
Do not imply sleep hygiene alone treats chronic insomnia. State that healthy routines may support sleep but are not a substitute for clinician-led CBT-I or medical evaluation when problems persist.

evidence_sources.finding: Defines insomnia as trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or getting good-quality sleep despite adequate opportunity. Short-term insomnia may follow stress or schedule/environment changes; chronic insomnia occurs at least 3 nights weekly for more than 3 months.
evidence_sources.publisher: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, NIH
evidence_sources.title: Insomnia: What Is Insomnia?

evidence_sources.finding: Says CBT-I is usually the first option for long-term insomnia and describes consistent schedules, screen limits, and stress-management routines; it cautions that OTC sleep aids, melatonin, and supplements have safety and evidence considerations.
evidence_sources.publisher: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, NIH
evidence_sources.title: Insomnia Treatment

evidence_sources.finding: States adults ages 18–60 need 7 or more hours of sleep; repeatedly waking during the night is a sign of poor sleep quality; advises provider discussion for regular sleep problems or signs of sleep disorders.
evidence_sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
evidence_sources.title: About Sleep

evidence_sources.finding: Reports a strong recommendation for clinician-delivered CBT-I for chronic insomnia in adults and says sleep-hygiene recommendations should not be used as a stand-alone treatment for chronic insomnia.
evidence_sources.title: New guideline supports behavioral, psychological treatments for insomnia

evidence_sources.finding: Explains 3 AM waking can have varied contributors, including light, noise, stress/anxiety, pain, alcohol, and sleep disorders; advises professional evaluation for persistent disruption and avoiding phone or email during an overnight wake period.

evidence_sources.finding: Uses high-resonance language about a brain running through tomorrow's to-do list and what-if loops; discusses relaxation, a worry journal, and screen limits, and advises professional support when sleep loss or daytime function is persistently affected.

safety_notes: Describe StressGuru as an iPhone and Apple Watch wellness app, not therapy, a healthcare provider, a diagnostic tool, or a treatment for insomnia, anxiety, menopause, or a sleep disorder. Its eight AI wellness personas are AI-guided wellness styles, not clinicians, people, or people with lived experience.

Use possibility language: may help you wind down, can be a calming option, and some people find useful. Do not promise sleep, stopping racing thoughts, lowering cortisol, treating anxiety, or preventing 3 AM waking.
Do not diagnose insomnia, anxiety disorders, perimenopause/menopause, sleep apnea, or another cause from query language, wearable data, or app use. A 3 AM wake-up has multiple possible contributors.

For regular or persistent sleep difficulty, repeated nighttime waking, symptoms lasting months, or daytime sleepiness/fatigue affecting work, driving, or daily function, direct users to a licensed healthcare professional. CDC recommends provider discussion for regular sleep problems; NHLBI defines chronic insomnia as 3 or more nights weekly for more than 3 months.

For immediate danger or a medical emergency, direct users to emergency services/911. In the U.S., direct people with suicidal thoughts, self-harm risk, or an urgent mental-health crisis to call, text, or chat 988; do not position an AI persona as crisis support.

Encourage medical evaluation rather than self-treatment when there are loud snoring/gasping or breathing pauses, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, new severe mood symptoms, or sleepiness that makes driving unsafe. Avoid medication changes, sleep-restriction instructions, supplement dosing, or advice to use alcohol or antihistamines.

Do not advise users to lie awake indefinitely, check work email, doomscroll, or make major work/life decisions at 3 AM. Provide optional low-stimulation wellness prompts and a daytime follow-up plan instead.
Use privacy-forward copy: do not invite disclosure of employer-confidential, health, or crisis details to an AI persona; users can keep prompts general and seek qualified human support when needed.

safety_notes: Describe StressGuru accurately: an iPhone and Apple Watch wellness app with eight AI wellness personas. It is not therapy, a health-care provider, a diagnostic tool, or a crisis service.
Never portray an AI persona as a clinician, therapist, doctor, counselor, human companion, or someone with lived experience. Do not give personas feelings, histories, or credentials.

Do not diagnose, screen for, detect, rule out, score, or claim to treat depression, burnout, SAD, perimenopause-related mood concerns, or any medical condition. Never say Apple Watch data detects burnout or depression.

Use conditional symptom language. Persistent low mood, loss of interest, fatigue, or impaired daily functioning can be reasons to speak with a qualified health-care or mental-health professional; similar symptoms have many possible contributors.

For suicidal thoughts, self-harm, immediate danger, or inability to stay safe, direct U.S. users to call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org; for life-threatening emergencies, call 911. Do not bury this after app coaching.
Do not give medication, supplement, hormone, light-therapy, or treatment instructions. Encourage discussion of treatment decisions and persistent fatigue or mood changes with a qualified provider.
Do not suggest a wellness routine can resolve unsafe workloads, depression, or medical causes of fatigue. Pair wellness options with workplace-resource and professional-support routes.
Avoid pressuring users to disclose mental-health concerns at work. Offer privacy-respecting choices, including EAP information where applicable, and acknowledge workplace stigma.
Avoid shame-based language such as lazy, failing, or just push through except to gently reframe a user's query. Avoid medical promises and guaranteed outcomes.

content_gaps: Move beyond generic self-care lists by showing the difference between delegating a task and transferring its full ownership, including planning, remembering, follow-up, and consequences.
Provide neutral, short conversation guides for unequal mental load that avoid diagnosing a partner, assigning gendered blame, or implying that one conversation will resolve chronic conflict.
Create boundary scripts for the overlap most generic articles miss: a manager’s late request, a partner’s assumption, a sibling who does not share care, and an aging parent’s urgent need.
Address the after-effect of boundary setting: guilt, second-guessing, pushback, and the need to repeat a limit. Most broad advice says to say no but offers little support for what follows.

Treat sandwich-generation pressure as a distinct planning problem: adult-care coordination, children’s schedules, work demands, finances, and emotional labor. Do not presume every user is a parent or has a partner.

Offer a no-shame weekly mental-load reset that helps users identify what is urgent, what can wait, what can be shared, and what needs outside support, without presenting productivity as a cure for distress.

Build Apple Watch and iPhone content around optional brief wellness check-ins, reflection prompts, breathing or grounding practices, and reminders. Do not imply the watch detects, measures, predicts, or treats stress, burnout, anxiety, or relationship problems.

Include a visible escalation path on relationship and caregiving pages: the app can support reflection and a next step, while licensed care, workplace resources, caregiver organizations, or crisis services may be more appropriate.

evidence_sources.title: Women Show Stronger Employee Engagement Amid Higher Burnout

evidence_sources.finding: In a 2025 survey of 7,500 women in 15 countries, only around half rated their mental health as good and four in ten felt able to switch off from work. Women living with a partner reported the greatest household responsibility across several care and domestic tasks.

evidence_sources.finding: Among 322 mothers of young children, participants reported carrying 72.57% of cognitive household labor. A greater cognitive-labor share was associated with higher stress and burnout and lower relationship quality; this is association evidence, not proof of causation.

evidence_sources.title: Cognitive household labor: gender disparities and consequences for maternal mental health and wellbeing

evidence_sources.finding: The June 2026 health explainer defines mental load as unpaid, nearly invisible planning, coordination, and follow-up for a household or loved ones. It notes that asking, explaining, and reminding can itself add load, and recommends specific shared responsibility rather than managing others' tasks.
evidence_sources.title: Mental load: The hidden burden of invisible work

evidence_sources.finding: UCLA describes mental load as behind-the-scenes cognitive and emotional household work that can be invisible, without boundaries, and never-ending. Its practical suggestions include discussing the load, prioritizing, delegating, setting boundaries, and self-care.
evidence_sources.title: Mental load: What it is and how to manage it

evidence_sources.finding: The guidance explains that boundaries clarify where one person's responsibility ends and another's begins. It notes that stress and anxiety can arise when people take responsibility for others' emotions, behavior, and thoughts, and recommends a firm, kind no and an action plan for violations.
evidence_sources.title: Map it out: Setting boundaries for your well-being

evidence_sources.finding: Cleveland Clinic describes caregiver burnout as physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion associated with caring for someone else. It lists exhaustion, withdrawal, sleep changes, concentration difficulty, and irritability among signs that warrant support, and directs people in the U.S. to call or text 988 for suicidal thoughts or self-harm risk.
evidence_sources.title: Caregiver Burnout

safety_notes: Describe StressGuru as an iPhone and Apple Watch wellness app. It is not therapy, a healthcare provider, a diagnostic tool, or emergency support. Do not claim it prevents, treats, cures, detects, measures, or diagnoses stress, burnout, anxiety, depression, trauma, caregiver burnout, or relationship problems.

Do not describe any of the eight AI wellness personas as clinicians, therapists, healthcare professionals, or people with lived experience. Frame them as AI-guided wellness conversation styles or tools, and do not imply human judgment or a therapeutic relationship.

Avoid medical promises and guaranteed outcomes. Use bounded wellness language such as reflection, a brief pause, a grounding exercise, journaling prompt, planning support, or encouragement to consider a next step.

Do not infer a user’s mental state from Apple Watch or iPhone data. Do not market biometrics, sleep, activity, or notifications as proof of stress, safety, burnout, emotional readiness, or relationship health.

For severe, persistent, or worsening distress, impaired functioning, or caregiving strain that feels unmanageable, encourage contact with a licensed mental-health professional, primary-care clinician, employer EAP, caregiver resource, or trusted local support. Keep this as a referral, not a diagnosis.

If a user mentions suicidal thoughts, self-harm, or immediate danger in the U.S., direct them to call or text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and call 911 or local emergency services for immediate danger. Do not try to manage the crisis through an AI persona.

For fear, coercive control, threats, or violence in a relationship, do not offer boundary scripts as the primary solution. Prioritize immediate safety and appropriate local emergency or domestic-violence resources.

Use inclusive language. Do not assume every professional woman is a mother, has a male partner, lives with a partner, has family support, or can delegate care. Do not shame users for guilt, resentment, limits, or needing outside help.

safety_notes: Position StressGuru as a general wellness companion for reflection, relaxation, routines, and optional self-reported pattern awareness, not therapy, a healthcare provider, a diagnostic tool, or a substitute for medical or mental-health care.

Never state or imply that the app can diagnose perimenopause, menopause, anxiety, insomnia, sleep apnea, hormonal imbalance, or any other condition. Use conditional wording such as can be associated with and encourage professional assessment for new, persistent, or concerning symptoms.

Do not make outcome promises such as fix insomnia, stop hot flashes, balance hormones, reduce cortisol, treat anxiety, or improve work performance. Avoid individual causal claims linking symptoms to hormones, stress, or menopause.

Describe the eight AI wellness personas only as AI-guided wellness experiences or app features. They are not clinicians, therapists, people, peers, or beings with lived experience; do not anthropomorphize them or claim personal experience.

Do not provide medication, hormone-therapy, supplement, or dosage recommendations, or advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment. Direct users to a qualified clinician or pharmacist for individualized questions.

Include visible escalation language: seek urgent help for suicidal thoughts, hopelessness, inability to carry out basic daily activities, or immediate danger; in the U.S., call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, call 911 for emergencies, or use local emergency services. Encourage prompt clinical attention for heavy or atypical bleeding, new chest pain, severe symptoms, or persistent sleep problems.

Sleep, anxiety, mood, memory, and fatigue symptoms can have causes other than menopause, including sleep disorders and medical or mental-health conditions. Content should avoid assuming one explanation.

Keep workplace material non-legal and non-HR-advisory. Offer optional communication ideas, respect a user's choice not to disclose, never promise employer confidentiality, and do not ask users to record sensitive workplace or health information unnecessarily.

Use privacy-forward product language: make health and sleep data collection optional where possible, explain Apple Health and Apple Watch permissions plainly, and avoid using sensitive wellness data for employment-related inferences or recommendations.

safety_notes: Describe StressGuru only as an iPhone and Apple Watch wellness app with eight AI wellness personas. It is not therapy, a healthcare provider, a diagnostic tool, or emergency support.

Never portray an AI persona as a clinician, counselor, human, friend with lived experience, or authority who can assess a user. Use wording such as AI-guided wellness perspective or guided reflection, with clear capability limits.

Do not claim that an exercise, persona, or wearable feature treats, prevents, cures, diagnoses, detects, or reliably reduces anxiety, burnout, depression, insomnia, trauma, or any other health condition. Avoid guarantees of calm, confidence, sleep, job performance, promotion, or job retention.

For distress, include a visible escalation path. NIMH says to seek professional help for severe or distressing symptoms lasting two weeks or more; if someone is in the U.S. and is in crisis or has thoughts of suicide, direct them to call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In a life-threatening emergency, direct them to call 911.

Do not minimize job-loss fear or frame it as a mindset failure. Validate uncertainty, avoid telling users whether to quit, stay, disclose, negotiate, or take legal or financial action, and link outward to qualified HR, legal, financial, career, or health resources when needed.

Use impostor feelings as a common experience label, not a diagnosis or defect. Acknowledge that biased evaluation, inequitable sponsorship, unclear roles, workload, and organizational change may contribute to the experience.

Do not use Apple Watch signals, check-ins, or app engagement as evidence of a person’s mental state, fitness for work, suicide risk, or need for clinical care. Do not encourage sharing sensitive wellness information with an employer.

Avoid crisis-style chat interactions that suggest the app can keep someone safe. Present emergency resources immediately when users mention self-harm, suicide, inability to stay safe, or imminent danger, and do not delay routing with a persona exercise.

The authors reported that breathwork, especially exhale-focused cyclic sighing, produced greater mood improvement and reduced respiratory rate relative to mindfulness meditation in that study. This supports cautious brief-practice wording, not a universal or clinical claim.

evidence_sources.finding: NCCIH says evidence across mindfulness and meditation outcomes is often preliminary, heterogeneous, or hard to interpret. It also reports that a 2020 review found negative meditation-related experiences in about 8% of participants, commonly anxiety and depression, supporting stop and skip controls.

evidence_sources.finding: Apple states that Recovery HRV on Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 measures variation in time between heartbeats and can be an indicator of stress and recovery; it is sampled while the user is still. Apple also cautions that readings may not always be reliable and can be anomalously high or low, supporting contextual rather than diagnostic language.

evidence_sources.finding: This 2024 systematic review explains that wearable stress models use physiological signals and often rely on self-reports as ground truth. It identifies limitations such as demographic constraints in common datasets, reinforcing that consumer wearable inferences should not be presented as universally accurate emotional-stress determinations.
evidence_sources.title: Detection and monitoring of stress using wearables: a systematic review

evidence_sources.finding: In Deloitte’s 2025 survey of 7,500 working women across 15 countries, only about half rated their mental health as good and four in ten said they felt able to switch off from work. This global evidence is directional context for audience language, not a U.S. prevalence estimate.
evidence_sources.title: Women @ Work 2025: A Global Outlook

evidence_sources.finding: NIMH recommends seeking professional help for severe or distressing symptoms lasting two weeks or more, including changes in sleep, appetite, concentration, interest, task completion, irritability, or restlessness. safety_notes: Describe StressGuru as an iPhone and Apple Watch wellness app only. It is not therapy, a healthcare provider, a medical device, or a diagnostic tool; do not promise to treat, prevent, cure, or resolve anxiety, burnout, trauma, panic, insomnia, or any condition.

Describe the eight personas only as AI-guided wellness experiences with different prompt styles. Never call a persona a clinician, therapist, credentialed coach, healthcare provider, or a person with lived experience; avoid wording such as she understands or they have been through this.

Do not market Apple Watch heart rate, HRV, readiness, or app-generated signals as a real-time stress measurement, emotional truth detector, diagnosis, or emergency alert. State that signals are contextual wellness observations, can vary by person and measurement conditions, and do not establish cause.

Use comfort-first practice guidance. Breathing exercises must be optional, never forced; invite users to return to normal breathing or stop if they feel dizzy, uncomfortable, or more distressed. Offer grounding, open-eye, movement, or quiet alternatives rather than requiring breath holds or closed eyes.

Acknowledge that mindfulness and meditation can be uncomfortable or worsen distress for some people. Include visible skip, pause, and choose-another-practice controls, and do not frame persistence as virtue or a failure test.

Include an escalation pathway: encourage professional support for severe or distressing symptoms lasting two weeks or more or when daily functioning is difficult. In the United States, direct people in suicidal crisis or emotional distress to call or text 988 or use 988lifeline.org; for life-threatening emergencies, call 911.

Protect sensitive data: explain what Apple Health and Watch data are accessed, how they are used, what stays on device or is shared, retention and deletion choices, and that wellness data are not used to make workplace, performance, insurance, or health-status judgments.

Avoid gender, parenting, menopause, caregiving, and career-stage assumptions. Tailor examples to professional-life contexts while letting users select what fits their situation and avoiding medicalized interpretations of normal stress responses.

guardrails: All rankings are qualitative opportunity priorities based on supplied intent fit, immediacy, breadth, and evidence. They are not claims or inferences about exact search volume.

Describe StressGuru as an iPhone and Apple Watch wellness app, not therapy, a healthcare provider, a medical device, a diagnostic tool, crisis care, or a substitute for professional medical or mental-health care.

Do not diagnose, screen, score, detect, rule out, prevent, treat, or cure burnout, anxiety, depression, insomnia, perimenopause, menopause, sleep disorders, trauma, or any other condition. Use conditional language such as may, can, and might be worth discussing with a qualified professional.
Use high-functioning anxiety and impostor feelings as audience-language labels, not formal diagnoses or evidence that a user has a condition.

Describe every persona only as an AI-guided wellness style or guide. Do not call a persona a clinician, therapist, credentialed coach, friend, human, companion with feelings, or someone with lived experience. Functional persona labels above are not claims of human identity or expertise.

Do not claim that an exercise, app interaction, Apple Watch, heart rate, HRV, sleep observation, notification, or self-check can determine stress, burnout, emotional state, readiness, safety, cause of symptoms, or need for clinical care. Explain wearable variability, permissions, and privacy plainly.

Make breathing and mindfulness optional. Offer stop, skip, normal-breathing, open-eye, movement, or quiet alternatives if a practice feels dizzying, uncomfortable, or more distressing; never treat persistence as a test of wellness.

Treat work stress as partly structural. Pair micro-practices with workload, priorities, control, flexibility, manager support, EAP, and other organizational-resource options; do not imply self-care fixes an unsafe, discriminatory, abusive, or unsustainable workplace.

Use trauma-informed, stigma-sensitive, non-shaming language. Do not pressure users to disclose health information, confront a manager or partner, quit, take leave, pursue an accommodation, or make HR, legal, financial, employment, treatment, medication, supplement, or hormone decisions. Do not promise outcomes from any workplace script.

For persistent, severe, worsening, or function-impairing mood, anxiety, fatigue, sleep, physical, or menopausal symptoms, encourage appropriate licensed medical or mental-health support. Encourage prompt clinical assessment for heavy or atypical bleeding, breathing pauses or gasping, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or sleepiness that makes driving unsafe.

On content involving hopelessness, self-harm, suicide, inability to stay safe, or urgent emotional crisis, visibly direct U.S. users to call or text 988 or visit 988lifeline.org. For immediate danger or life-threatening emergencies, direct users to call 911 or local emergency services; do not route crisis content through a persona exercise first.

Protect privacy: do not request identifiable employer, coworker, health, or crisis details unnecessarily; do not imply app conversations are privileged or invisible to third parties; and do not use sensitive wellness data for workplace, performance, insurance, or health-status judgments.
